On October 15, on a training range at Fort Knox, Kentucky, the U.S. military tried something that sounds like science fiction and isn't. At U.S. European Command's request, DARPA sent out a team of four self-driving robots to hunt for enemy positions on their own. The whole point was to test an idea the Pentagon is taking seriously: sending machines into a fight ahead of human soldiers. Fort Knox was chosen because its terrain can stand in for a European battlefield.

Here's how it played out. An operator received satellite imagery of a suspected enemy position and pointed the robotic team at it. One vehicle rolled forward alone, using its own sensors to search, and when it spotted a likely position, it stopped and waited for orders. Two more robots moved up to support it, and a simulated rocket struck the target about 300 yards away. The lead vehicle even carried a drone it could launch to scout ahead or strike. The machines can also haul supplies and ammunition, or carry wounded soldiers out.

One part matters more than anything else, and the military was clear about it: the robots drive and spot targets on their own, but a human still makes the decision to fire. As DARPA technical adviser Jason Gregory put it, the systems handle the moving and the detecting, but "they don't pull the trigger until a human says pull the trigger." The autonomy is in getting there and finding the enemy, not in deciding to use force.

The reason behind all of this sits on NATO's eastern edge. The effort is part of what's called the Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative, and the concept is blunt: a force of robots, drones, and sensors that would absorb the first blow if a NATO country were invaded, soaking up the opening hits so that human troops don't have to. It is aimed squarely at the possibility of a Russian move against the alliance, and it draws directly on lessons from Ukraine, where cheap drones and unmanned systems have rewritten how wars are fought. The idea was championed by recently retired Gen. Christopher Donahue.

It's still early. Right now the robots can drive themselves, scout, and wait for orders, and the next round of testing in December will put real soldiers alongside them to see how it actually works. No one is replacing troops with machines. But the direction is clear, and a little startling: the United States is seriously preparing for a day when the first thing an invading army runs into on NATO's frontier isn't a soldier, but a robot built to take the hit in a soldier's place.

Something happened over the Mediterranean last week that had never happened before. On October 20 and 21, France and the United Kingdom flew their first-ever joint airborne nuclear-strike exercise, codenamed "Rummy." Royal Air Force Eurofighter Typhoons escorted French Rafale jets on a simulated nuclear-strike mission out of Saint-Dizier air base in eastern France. No actual warheads were involved, it was a rehearsal, but the fact that it happened at all is the story.

To understand why it matters, you have to know how fiercely independent France has always been about its nuclear forces. Its Strategic Air Forces have operated alone since the 1960s, answering to Paris and no one else. One analyst called flying a nuclear mission alongside another country a "revolution." It grows out of the Northwood Declaration, signed in July 2025, in which France and Britain agreed to coordinate their nuclear forces and declared there is no extreme threat to Europe that wouldn't draw a response from both of them.

Here's why Americans should care. This is happening because Europe is nervous. With open questions about how reliable the U.S. nuclear umbrella will be in the years ahead, and a Russia that keeps rattling its own arsenal next door, Europe's only two nuclear powers are quietly building a backup. France calls the broader idea "forward deterrence." In plain terms, two of America's closest allies are rehearsing how to protect the continent with or without Washington.

They're careful to say they aren't merging their forces. "Having independent nuclear forces doesn't exclude coordination," said French Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin. Both countries keep their own weapons and their own launch decisions, which they do not share. France brings something Britain doesn't have, an airborne leg, with Rafales that carry nuclear-tipped cruise missiles; the UK's deterrent rides entirely on submarines. So this exercise paired France's air-launched punch with British jets flying guard.

For most of the last 80 years, the security of Western Europe has rested, ultimately, on the American guarantee. Two allies rehearsing a nuclear strike together, without the U.S. in the cockpit, is a quiet but real signal that they are preparing to stand on their own if they ever have to. Whether you find that reassuring or unsettling depends on where you sit. Either way, it's a shift worth watching, because it says as much about trust in America as it does about France and Britain.

That New Bradley Smell

How's this for a new ride? Pfc. James Hays gets behind the wheel of a newly fielded M2A4E1 Bradley Fighting Vehicle. The fielding equips the brigade with upgraded Bradleys featuring improved protection, targeting and environmental-control capabilities.

There's a chain of islands that curves from Japan down past Taiwan to the Philippines, and the U.S. military calls it the first island chain. It sits right on China's doorstep to the Pacific, and the U.S. Army has spent the last few years quietly turning it into a line of long-range firing positions. The idea is simple: if China ever tried to push American forces out of the Western Pacific, the Army wants launchers already sitting inside that zone, able to reach out and hold ships and targets at risk.

The headliner is a system called Typhon, the Army's Mid-Range Capability. It fires the SM-6 at air and sea targets a few hundred miles out, and the Tomahawk at land targets as far as roughly 1,000 miles. It first went to the Philippines in 2024, at Manila's request, and it has stayed. Army commanders say Typhon has now held a forward presence there for more than 30 straight months. This past May, during an exercise, a Typhon launcher fired a Tomahawk that flew nearly 400 miles across Luzon and struck its target.

Working alongside it is a system most people already know: HIMARS, the wheeled rocket launcher. It can hit targets on land and at sea, and the Army has been moving it across the map, Palawan facing the South China Sea, northern Luzon facing Taiwan, and islands in Japan's southwest. At this year's Balikatan exercise in the Philippines, HIMARS rolled onto Itbayat, an island only about 100 miles from Taiwan, and later carried out its first live-fire drill on Philippine soil to practice protecting nearby shipping lanes.

Behind all of it is one worry: China has built an enormous arsenal designed to keep the U.S. Navy and Air Force at arm's length in any Pacific fight. By scattering launchers across friendly islands, the Army is trying to make that harder, and to give any opponent, as U.S. Army Pacific commander Gen. Ronald Clark put it, reason to "pause." A newly stood-up command, the 7th Infantry Division's Multi-Domain Command-Pacific, now ties the ground troops and the long-range fires together under one roof.

It's not a finished picture, and it isn't a simple one. Keeping small, remote islands supplied in a real fight is a genuinely hard problem, and the Army's own war games keep flagging it. Beijing calls the exercises provocative and argues that tiny, exposed islands would be easy to spot and cut off. All of that is fair. But the message the U.S. is sending is hard to miss: it doesn't intend to watch a Pacific crisis from the far side of the ocean. It intends to already be standing inside the first island chain when it starts.

Every so often the U.S. Air Force puts a number on the future, and it just did. In a force-structure report sent to Congress on October 16, the service laid out the fighter force it believes it will need by 2035: about 1,509 combat-coded fighters, and a lineup that looks noticeably different from the one flying today.

The F-35 becomes the backbone. It would grow to roughly 40 percent of the fleet, up from about 30 percent now. At the high end, the F-22 Raptor and the brand-new F-47, the Air Force's next-generation stealth fighter, would together make up about 20 percent, with the F-47 essentially replacing the Raptor one-for-one as it retires. The remaining 40 percent would be split between the F-15 and the F-16, the workhorses that have carried the force for decades.

Some familiar jets are on the way out. The oldest F-16s reach the end of their flying lives in the mid-2030s, and whether to buy a fresh batch of new-build F-16s is still undecided. And the one that will sting for a lot of people: the A-10 Warthog, the beloved close-air-support tank-buster, isn't part of the 2035 plan at all. After years of the Air Force trying to retire it and Congress fighting to keep it, this plan quietly leaves it out.

The biggest shift isn't even counted in that 1,509 number. The Air Force is also building Collaborative Combat Aircraft, uncrewed "drone wingmen" meant to fly alongside piloted jets, carry sensors, and take on the riskiest tasks. The service wants 500 of them by 2032, and officials have signaled that as those drones come online, the number of crewed fighters it needs could actually fall.

None of this is locked in. The plan assumes "medium" risk, meaning the force could be stretched in a long war, and it leans on budgets that aren't settled, part of next year's F-35 buy hinges on a funding bill still moving through Congress. To make it all work, industry has to build about 72 new fighters a year, and the Air Force says the companies have promised they can. As one general put it, "we believe them." Caveats and all, it's the clearest look yet at what American airpower is supposed to look like a decade from now.

Are you a robot? Or are you lethal?

In the high-stakes environments where our service members operate, grit and readiness are the only verifications that matter.
